USA.gov: A president chosen through the electoral college runs the government, and a separately elected Congress writes the laws. Congress has two parts: the House, where bigger states get more seats, and the Senate, where every state gets two. Courts can strike down laws that break the constitution. It's a federal system, so all 50 states also have their own governors and laws.
USA.vote: House members serve two years, senators six, and presidents four. Most seats go to whoever gets the most votes, which is called first-past-the-post. The president isn't chosen by the nationwide vote total but by the electoral college: each state gets a number of electors, and nearly all states give every elector to whoever wins that state. Each state runs its own elections, so the rules vary.
USA.history: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776. They argued over how much power a central government should have, and in 1787 wrote the constitution still used today. Small and large states compromised: seats in one chamber by population, and equal seats in the other. The right to vote started narrow and grew over time, reaching Black men on paper in 1870, women in 1920, and enforced Black voting rights in 1965.

timeline.t: Black men given the vote on paper
Women win the right to vote
Voting Rights Act enforces Black voting rights

CAN.gov: Voters elect a parliament. The leader of the party that can win its support becomes prime minister. King Charles is head of state, but his job is mostly for show, and a governor general stands in for him. Ten provinces have strong powers of their own, including over health and schools.
CAN.vote: Canadians vote in 343 local areas called ridings. Whoever gets the most votes in a riding wins it, which is first-past-the-post. The Senate isn't elected: its members are appointed. The constitution allows up to five years between elections, a law sets four, and they're often called sooner.
CAN.history: Indigenous nations already lived here when France and Britain both set up colonies. Britain took control in 1763. In 1867 several colonies joined to form a self-governing country under the Crown. Canada got full control of its own constitution only in 1982. Quebec, which mostly speaks French, has voted twice on leaving. It stayed both times.

timeline.t: Canada gains full control of its constitution
Quebec votes on leaving and stays

MEX.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government for one six-year term and can never run again. Congress has a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies. Mexico has 31 states plus Mexico City, which has much the same powers.
MEX.vote: The president wins with the most votes, with no runoff. Lawmakers are chosen by a mix: some win local districts, and others get seats based on their party's share of the vote. The single-term rule for presidents is one of the country's firmest political traditions.
MEX.history: Spain conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521 and ruled Mexico for three centuries. Independence came in 1821. Then came years of chaos, foreign invasions and a long dictatorship. A revolution began in 1910. Its winners formed the party that held the presidency for 71 years. That ended peacefully in 2000, when an opposition candidate won.

timeline.t: Ruling party formed after the revolution

GTM.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government for one four-year term, and a Congress with one chamber. A president can't run again.
GTM.vote: If no presidential candidate wins a majority, the top two go to a runoff. Congress seats are shared out by each party's vote share. Critics have at times accused courts and election officials of interfering with candidates, which has been a major source of conflict.
GTM.history: Guatemala was the center of Spain's rule in Central America, and became independent in 1821. A coup backed by the US overthrew its elected president in 1954, and a civil war lasted from 1960 to 1996. Peace accords ended the war in 1996.

BLZ.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the leader of the winning party becomes prime minister. King Charles is head of state, but only for show. A governor general stands in for him.
BLZ.vote: Whoever gets the most votes in each local area wins its seat in the House of Representatives. The Senate is appointed. Two main parties have traded power for decades.
BLZ.history: Belize was once part of the Maya world. It later became a British colony called British Honduras. It won independence in 1981, the last British colony on the American mainland. Guatemala has long claimed part of its land, and the world's top court is now looking at the dispute.

timeline.t: Becomes the colony of British Honduras

SLV.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, and a Legislative Assembly with one chamber. Observers say power has moved heavily to the president in recent years. Court rulings and a 2025 change to the constitution now let presidents run again with no limit.
SLV.vote: Until now a president needed a majority or faced a runoff; from 2027 the most votes wins in one round, and the term becomes six years. The 60 Assembly seats are shared out by party vote share. Critics inside and outside the country warn that checks on the president have weakened, while supporters point to a steep fall in gang violence.
SLV.history: A civil war ran from 1979 to 1992 between the army-led government and left-wing rebels. A peace deal ended it, and the rebels became a political party. For decades two parties took turns in power. In 2019 a president won by promising to break their hold. He later launched a harsh crackdown on gangs.

HND.gov: Voters elect a president to run the government and a National Congress with one chamber. Most power sits with the national government, not with local areas.
HND.vote: The president wins with the most votes in one round, with no runoff. Congress seats are shared by party vote share, and voters can pick individual candidates across party lists.
HND.history: Honduras has been free of Spain since 1821. It had many army governments in the 1900s, and US banana companies had huge influence. Civilian rule came back in 1982. A 2009 coup removed the president, and disputed elections have caused trouble since.

NIC.gov: On paper, voters elect a president and a National Assembly. In real life, President Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, hold almost all the power. Changes to the constitution now make them co-presidents.
NIC.vote: Elections are held, but top opposition candidates were jailed before the 2021 vote. Many observers from other countries rejected the results. Thousands of critics have been forced to leave or have lost their citizenship.
NIC.history: The Somoza family ruled as dictators for over 40 years, until the left-wing Sandinista revolution of 1979. A US-backed rebel force, the Contras, then fought the Sandinistas through the 1980s. Voters removed Ortega in 1990. He returned to power in 2007 and has since steadily dismantled limits on it.

CRI.gov: Voters elect a president and a Legislative Assembly with one chamber. Costa Rica got rid of its army in 1948. It has only police.
CRI.vote: A presidential candidate needs at least 40% of the vote, or the top two go to a runoff. The 57 Assembly seats are shared by party vote share in each province. Lawmakers can't run for immediate re-election. Voting is compulsory in law but not enforced.
CRI.history: A short civil war was fought in 1948. The winners wrote a new constitution, got rid of the army and gave the vote to women and Black citizens. Costa Rica has been one of Latin America's steadiest democracies ever since.

timeline.t: Civil war ends and the army is abolished
Women and Black citizens get the vote

PAN.gov: Voters elect a president for one five-year term, and a National Assembly with one chamber. A president can't run again right away.
PAN.vote: The president wins with the most votes in one round, with no runoff. The 71 Assembly members are chosen in local districts, some electing one member and some several.
PAN.history: Panama separated from Colombia in 1903 with US backing, and the US then built the canal and controlled the land around it. Military ruler Manuel Noriega was removed by a US invasion in 1989. Panama took over full control of the canal at the end of 1999.

timeline.t: Separates from Colombia with US backing
Panama takes full control of the canal

CUB.gov: The Communist Party is the only legal party, and the constitution names it the leading force in society. The party's first secretary holds the most power. There's also a president, chosen by the National Assembly.
CUB.vote: People do vote for the National Assembly, but each seat has only one candidate. Committees firmly controlled by the Communist Party pick those candidates. Voters can back all, some or none of them, but can't vote against anyone, and no rival parties campaign. The government calls this its own kind of democracy. Critics say voters have no real choice.
CUB.history: Spain gave up Cuba after a war in 1898. The US ran it until 1902. Cuba then became independent, but under strong US influence. Dictator Fulgencio Batista later ran it, until Fidel Castro's revolution took power in 1959 and sided with the Soviet Union. The US has blocked most trade since 1960, which Cuba's government calls a blockade. Fidel led until 2006 and his brother Raul until 2018. Raul stayed head of the Communist Party until 2021.

timeline.t: Cuba becomes independent after US rule

HTI.gov: The constitution calls for an elected president, prime minister and parliament. In real life, Haiti has had no elected national leaders for years. A temporary council held the presidency from 2024 until February 2026. Since then a prime minister has led the government, while armed gangs control much of the capital.
HTI.vote: Haiti last held national elections in 2016. New ones have been repeatedly promised and delayed, and are now scheduled for July 2027. When held, they use a two-round system.
HTI.history: Haiti won independence in 1804, after enslaved people rose up against French rule. It was the first republic led by Black people. France later demanded money in return for recognizing it, and historians say that debt hurt its economy for generations. Dictatorship, coups, a US occupation, a 2010 earthquake and the killing of its president in 2021 followed.

timeline.t: Transitional council takes over the presidency

DOM.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies.
DOM.vote: A president needs more than half the votes, or the top two meet in a runoff. Deputies are chosen by party vote share, and each province elects one senator.
DOM.history: The country shares an island with Haiti. The dictator Rafael Trujillo ruled from 1930 until he was killed in 1961. After years of unrest and a US intervention in 1965, it slowly became a stable democracy.

JAM.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the leader of the winning party becomes prime minister. King Charles is head of state, but only for show. Jamaica has talked about becoming a republic.
JAM.vote: Jamaica uses first-past-the-post across 63 local areas. Two parties have led politics ever since independence. Senators are appointed, not elected.
JAM.history: Spain and then Britain ruled the island, where enslaved Africans were forced to work on sugar plantations until slavery ended in the 1830s. Jamaica became independent in 1962.

BHS.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the leader of the winning party becomes prime minister. King Charles is the ceremonial head of state.
BHS.vote: Local areas each elect one member by first-past-the-post. Two main parties have traded power, and governments often change at elections.
BHS.history: The islands were a British colony for centuries, known for pirates and later for tourism and banking. Majority rule came in 1967 and independence in 1973.

BRB.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister runs the government. Barbados became a republic in 2021. A president picked by parliament replaced the British monarch as head of state.
BRB.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post. Results can be very one-sided: one party has won every seat in several recent elections.
BRB.history: England took Barbados as a colony in 1627, and its sugar farms relied on enslaved Africans. Slavery ended in the 1830s, and independence came in 1966. Its parliament is one of the oldest in the Americas.

TTO.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister runs the government. A president, picked by lawmakers, is head of state, but only for show.
TTO.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post. Politics has often split between people of African and Indian descent.
TTO.history: Spain and then Britain ruled these two islands. Workers were brought from India after slavery ended, shaping today's mixed society. Independence came in 1962, and a republic in 1976.

ATG.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister leads the government. King Charles is the ceremonial head of state.
ATG.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post. The Senate is appointed.
ATG.history: Antigua and Barbuda was a British colony built on sugar and slavery. It became independent in 1981. One family, the Birds, led politics for decades.

DMA.gov: Voters elect a parliament, which picks a president whose job is mostly for show. The prime minister runs the government.
DMA.vote: Most members win their local areas by first-past-the-post. A few more are appointed. Dominica is mostly rural and relies heavily on farming and tourism.
DMA.history: France and Britain fought over the island, which Britain held from 1763. It was one of the last Caribbean places where the Indigenous Kalinago kept territory. Independence came in 1978.

GRD.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister leads the government. King Charles is the ceremonial head of state.
GRD.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post, which has sometimes given one party every seat.
GRD.history: Grenada became independent from Britain in 1974. A revolution in 1979 brought a left-wing government. After a violent split inside it in 1983, the US invaded and brought back elections.

KNA.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister leads the government. King Charles is the ceremonial head of state. The smaller island, Nevis, has its own government and a right to leave.
KNA.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post. Nevis voted on leaving in 1998, but fell short of the two-thirds needed.
KNA.history: St. Kitts was the first English colony in the Caribbean, founded in 1623. The two islands became independent together in 1983.

LCA.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister leads the government. King Charles is the ceremonial head of state.
LCA.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post. Two main parties trade power.
LCA.history: France and Britain fought over Saint Lucia so often that it changed hands 14 times. Britain kept it from 1814, and independence came in 1979.

VCT.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister leads the government. King Charles is the ceremonial head of state. Voters rejected becoming a republic in 2009.
VCT.vote: Local areas elect members by first-past-the-post, and some seats are appointed.
VCT.history: The Garifuna people fought off colonizers for a long time. Britain then took control and sent many of them away in 1797. Independence came in 1979.

COL.gov: Voters elect a president for one four-year term, along with a Senate and a House of Representatives. Courts and independent bodies are very strong here.
COL.vote: The president needs a majority, or the top two go to a runoff. Congress seats are shared by party vote share. Special seats are set aside for Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities.
COL.history: Colombia won independence from Spain in 1819. A decades-long war between the government, left-wing rebels, right-wing armed groups and drug gangs has killed hundreds of thousands. A 2016 peace deal ended the war with the largest rebel group, but other armed groups remain.

VEN.gov: On paper, Venezuela has an elected president and a National Assembly. In real life, its government has gathered up a lot of power. Many accuse it of controlling the courts, the army and election officials.
VEN.vote: Voters use machines, and the president wins with the most votes. In 2024, Nicolás Maduro was declared the winner without the detailed results being published, and the opposition published tallies showing he lost. Many countries rejected the official result.
VEN.history: Simón Bolívar led the fight to break from Spain in the early 1800s. Venezuela grew rich from oil and was a stable democracy from 1958. Hugo Chávez won in 1998 promising to help the poor, and began a socialist project. After he died in 2013, the economy collapsed and millions of people left. In January 2026, a US military operation seized Maduro, and his vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, took over.

GUY.gov: Voters choose between party lists for parliament. The leader of the winning list automatically becomes president and runs the government.
GUY.vote: Everyone votes for a party rather than a person, and seats are shared by vote share. Politics has long split along lines between people of Indian and African descent. Oil discoveries have raised the stakes.
GUY.history: Dutch and then British colonizers brought enslaved Africans and later workers from India. Independence came in 1966. Venezuela claims a large part of Guyana's land, and the world's top court is now looking at the dispute.

SUR.gov: Voters elect a National Assembly. It then chooses the president, who runs the government.
SUR.vote: A president needs two-thirds of the Assembly. If nobody gets that, a wider group of local officials decides. Seats are shared out by each party's votes within districts.
SUR.history: Suriname was a Dutch colony until 1975. An army officer, Dési Bouterse, took power in a 1980 coup and later came back as an elected president. He was found guilty over the killing of opponents.

ECU.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, and a National Assembly with one chamber. In a crisis, a president can shut down the Assembly, but that also forces a new election for president.
ECU.vote: A candidate wins by getting over 50%, or 40% with a 10-point lead. Otherwise there's a runoff. Voting is compulsory for most adults.
ECU.history: Ecuador left Gran Colombia in 1830. Long unstable, it saw several presidents pushed out by protests in the 1990s and 2000s. In recent years, violence linked to drug gangs has become the country's top political issue.

PER.gov: Voters elect a president and a Congress with two chambers. Congress can remove a president for 'moral incapacity'. It has done so again and again, which has led to many presidents in just a few years.
PER.vote: A president needs a majority, or the top two go to a runoff. Congress seats are shared by party vote share. Voting is compulsory.
PER.history: Peru was the heart of the Inca Empire before the Spanish conquest. It saw long military rule, and a brutal war with Shining Path rebels in the 1980s and 90s. President Alberto Fujimori was later jailed, and the country has lurched between short-lived governments since.

BOL.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, and lawmakers in two chambers. The constitution names Bolivia's many Indigenous nations.
BOL.vote: A president wins with over 50%, or 40% with a 10-point lead, or else there's a runoff. Voting is compulsory.
BOL.history: Named after Simón Bolívar, Bolivia became independent in 1825, and has had many coups. Evo Morales, its first Indigenous president, won in 2005. A disputed 2019 election led to his resignation. His party won again in 2020, then lost power in 2025.

BRA.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, and a National Congress with two chambers. Brazil is a huge country of 26 states and a federal district, and each has powers of its own.
BRA.vote: If no one wins a majority for president, the top two go to a runoff. Voting is compulsory for adults, and uses electronic machines. So many parties win seats that presidents must always build coalitions.
BRA.history: Portugal made Brazil a colony. It became an independent empire in 1822 and a republic in 1889. It was the last country in the Americas to end slavery, in 1888. An army dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985. Today's constitution dates from 1988.

PRY.gov: Voters elect a president for one five-year term, with no second term, along with a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies.
PRY.vote: The president wins with the most votes in one round. Voting is compulsory. The Colorado Party has held power almost continuously for more than 70 years.
PRY.history: Paraguay lost a huge share of its people in the War of the Triple Alliance, from 1864 to 1870. General Alfredo Stroessner ruled as a dictator from 1954 to 1989. Elections with many parties then came back.

URY.gov: Voters elect a president and a General Assembly with two chambers. Uruguay is often ranked among the strongest democracies in Latin America.
URY.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. Seats are shared by party vote share, and voting is compulsory. Citizens can also force national referendums.
URY.history: Uruguay became independent in 1828, with Brazil and Argentina on either side. It built a strong welfare system early on, but an army dictatorship ruled from 1973 to 1985. Democracy came back and has stayed strong.

ARG.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, and a National Congress with two chambers. Argentina has 23 provinces plus Buenos Aires, and each has powers of its own.
ARG.vote: A president wins with 45%, or 40% with a 10-point lead. Otherwise there's a runoff. Half of the lower house is elected every two years, so midterms matter a lot. Voting is compulsory.
ARG.history: Argentina has been free of Spain since 1816. It grew rich, then swung between Juan Perón's strong political movement and army coups. A dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 made thousands of people disappear. Economic crises have shaped politics ever since democracy came back.

CHL.gov: Voters elect a president for one four-year term, along with a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies. A president can't serve two terms in a row.
CHL.vote: The president needs a majority, or the top two go to a runoff. Congress seats are shared by party vote share within districts. Voting was made compulsory again in 2022.
CHL.history: Chile has been independent since 1818 and had a long history of democracy. General Augusto Pinochet overthrew President Salvador Allende in 1973. His dictatorship lasted until a 1988 vote removed him. Chile still uses a constitution from that time, changed many times. Voters rejected two new ones.
